summary: A first-person account of how Sarah Gibson's bakery, Sweet Green in Middleton, overhauled its operations for sustainability. It covers local sourcing, energy-efficient equipment, compostable packaging, green certification, customer education, pricing transparency and networking. The piece argues that small businesses can balance profit and planet and inspire neighboring businesses.
one_line: Sweet Green, a Middleton bakery owned by Sarah Gibson, shows how a small business can adopt sustainability while staying profitable and inspiring others.
key_facts: The author visited Sweet Green, a bakery in the town of Middleton, on September 7, 2023.
Sweet Green is owned by Sarah Gibson, who began her sustainability journey with an audit of suppliers and packaging.
Sweet Green collaborated with nearby farmers for in-season products, reducing transportation emissions and ensuring freshness and quality.
In mid-October, Sweet Green implemented energy-efficient equipment, a significant upfront investment that is already lowering energy bills.
Sarah Gibson described single-use plastic packaging as a "modern-day Gordian knot."
Negotiations and bulk purchases from local sustainable packaging producers gave Sweet Green a cost-effective compostable packaging solution.
Sweet Green's pastries are now served in plant-based packaging that customers can compost at home.
Sweet Green received a green certification on November 3, 2023, after a process Sarah called rigorous.
Sarah reports an uptick in business from eco-aware consumers after the certification.
Sweet Green started workshops and 'green baking days' to educate customers and build loyalty.
Sweet Green talked frankly with customers about pricing reflecting the true cost of sustainable production, which drew even more people in.
Sarah Gibson joined sustainability networks and local green-initiative groups for motivation, knowledge exchange and support.
Other small businesses in Middleton began adopting eco-friendly practices after Sweet Green's example.
